title: LeBron James’ task in Philly bears a striking similarity to his new children’s book
content: Attention Philly shoppers: When you’re hitting the candy aisle this week for Halloween provisions, be sure to stock up on Twizzlers, Mike & Ike’s, Snickers and Reese’s. Should LeBron James opt to park his helicopter on your front stoop to trick-or-treat, that’s what he’ll be looking for. So says James via an email interview with CNN Sports about his latest book, “Happy Spooky Halloween.” The book, a simple story about big kids and little kids working together to craft a Halloween party that finds the balance between scary and fun, could be a metaphor for his current condition. Rewriting the NBA pecking order while relocating from Los Angeles to Philadelphia and trading the Lakers’ gold standard for the 76ers’ un-Processing is a little scary. But if the big kids (James, Jaylen Brown and Joel Embiid) work together with the little kids (Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe and Anfernee Simons), it also might be a lot of fun. To be clear, James wasn’t penning an autobiography here. Main character Zara’s quick work toning down the overzealous fifth-grade cast of flying witches and hungry wolves required a lot less effort than taming the New York Knicks and the Boston Celtics. He was merely writing a book about one of his favorite holidays, one that conjures fond memories of running around Akron, Ohio, dressed up like his favorite horror movie characters – the haunting, bladed-glove-handed Freddy Krueger from “A Nightmare on Elm Street,” the shapeshifting creepy clown Pennywise from Stephen King’s “It,” and the hockey-masked stalker Jason Voorhees (props to James for using both names when he referenced him) from “Friday the 13th.” But in its pages, James was also hoping to find another way to connect with kids. “When I was little, I remember how much joy it brought me to get out of the house and trick or treat, just to see what other people are dressed up as and get a bunch of candy,” he said. “I think there’s so much to love about that experience of everyone coming out and enjoying that tradition with your community.” Helping kids, connecting with them and inspiring them has been an ongoing theme of James’ off-court life. He has penned four children’s books, and eight years ago, his foundation provided the funding for the I Promise School , an Akron-based elementary school for at-risk children that now includes grades one through eight. “We want to inspire kids to read more, and to be encouraged by stories they see themselves in,” he said. Without settling too comfortably into the psychiatrist’s armchair, it is easy to see why James’ own life might fuel such a hope. It’s hard to remember James’ beginnings anymore. He’s 41, so those early days feel like a lifetime ago. But they’re also a lifestyle ago, a foggy memory so incongruent with the present that it is hard to imagine that we’re talking about the same person. LeBron James is one-name famous, a crossover star who made his name and fortune in sports yet became so otherworldly at playing basketball that his singular name became part of the world’s lexicon. But before all that – before the four rings and the three gold medals, before the estimated $1 billion in endorsements and the helicopter taxi, before The Chosen One evolved into King James – he was just the son of a single mom, growing up in search of roots in Akron. With the benefit of hindsight, knowing what we now know about James, his origin story reads more like a tall tale. There’s the 9-year-old living with a local football coach who walked into the backyard in October 1994 and took to hooping like a duck to water, and there’s the peewee football star who scored 18 touchdowns in his first six-game season. There’s the high school star so popular that they moved his games to the University of Akron arena to accommodate the crowds, and of course the teenager who ended up on the cover of Sports Illustrated. James was, goes the narrative, born for this and borne into this. But it was not that linear. Not even close. Lost in the hyperbole and foreshadowing of greatness is the hard and ordinary stuff. The son of a loving single mom who struggled to make a way for the boy they called BronBron. Sleeping on sofas, cashing welfare checks for snacks, and relying on strangers’ kindness to take him in gave him some semblance of stability and structure. The elementary schooler so lost that, in one single year, he missed, according to ESPN.com , more than 100 days of school – not because he didn’t want to learn but in part because his life was so transient, he wasn’t sure which school to go to. Back then, he read the “Goosebumps ” series as “an escape.” “Through books,” he told CNN Sports , “I could travel the world.’’ That inspired a life of curiosity, fueling an education not dissimilar to the one he’s trying to offer kids through his books. “I’m just a student of life and always want to learn new things,” he said. “So, I like to read about other people’s successes and journeys to see how they got to be where they are now.” He wasn’t being literal. But maybe have those sweets ready in case that candy-seeking helicopter shows up out front.

title: Family row over George Michael items up for auction - including Faith guitar
content:
A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.
The guitar played by the singer-songwriter in the Faith music video is one of several items being auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant.
Siobhan died in 2014 and the items are being sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.
Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Both Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.
Sworders describes the 32 lots as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".
Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.
Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.
Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.
There is no suggestion that Belcher does not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.
Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.
In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considers the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name is "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".
He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" is "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".
Bailey has asked that the auction should not go ahead, or, if it does, that it be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.
Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.
She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.
"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.
"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."
The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.
The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.
In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
content:
The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.
The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.
Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.
"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.
Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
A spokesperson for Greenville Police Department could not comment on what the DEA was investigating when contacted by the BBC.
Panettiere, who had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse , was found unresponsive in a South Carolina residence on 16 August.
Last month, the Greenville County Coroner's Office confirmed the former child star had died from an accidental drug overdose that included fentanyl - a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone.
The coroner also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an anti-psychotic medication used to treat certain mental health conditions.
The coroner's office had said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma" contributing to her death.
Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with her when emergency services arrived, according to a police report from the day she died.

title: Babydoll singer says life will 'never be the same again' after UK number one
content:
Jamie Miller says "nothing feels normal" anymore but he is trying to "live in the moment" as he comes to terms with his history-making song Babydoll.
Last week the 29-year-old became the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with the viral TikTok hit .
The singer, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, said his dreams had "come true" and life would "never be the same again" after a challenging few years in which he even had to give up on music for a time.
Miller said the last year had been "insane" as he has gone from watching Gavin and Stacey with his parents to getting messages on his social media from the cast.
Miller made history when he became the first Welsh artist to top the singles chart since Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.
He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone.
"It just doesn't feel real. To actually live my dreams the way that it's coming about right now," he said.
The song found fame on TikTok when actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos featuring the track. But Miller said the "genuineness" of the track also made it stand out as his first song since his hiatus.
"I went through a really, really hard few years  in my personal life, and I took two years off music," he said.
"There's a genuineness to how I sound in the song. The world's in a little bit of a dark place right now so maybe that's why it's made people come together."
Miller's song has shot him to stardom but, of course, life carries on as normal for his loved ones.
He said his parents were "finding it a bit mad" with his dad going back to work as an Uber driver in Cardiff.
"None of us know what's going on," he said.
"I remember sitting on the couch with my mum and dad last Christmas and we were all watching Gavin and Stacey.
"Now Ruth Jones and James Corden are commenting on my posts."
Last weekend Miller and Off Campus star Antonio Cipriano brought Babydoll to Strictly Come Dancing which left the Welsh star feeling a "little emotional" as he reconnected with Emma Willis.
He describes the presenter as one of his "biggest champions" in the last decade. She previously hosted The Voice UK when Miller got to the final in 2017.
He added: "It felt fulfilling to go up to her and say that I made something of myself.
"I've watched Strictly Come Dancing growing up and that's obviously been such a dream of mine to perform on the show."
Miller said now he wanted to "marry the two worlds of dancing and singing" in his career.

title: Government minister calls for review of 'unacceptable' BBC Scotland channel closure
content:
Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan has urged Ofcom to review "wholly unacceptable" plans to close the linear BBC Scotland channel.
The BBC last week announced the dedicated Scotland channel - as well as BBC Three and Radio 4 Extra - would move online as part of measures to make £500m of savings by 2028.
McAllan said moving the channel online would "reverse progress in improving the visibility and representation of Scotland within the UK's broadcasting landscape".
She called on Ofcom, the UK's independent broadcasting regulator, to scrutinise the decision and its implications.
McAllan wrote: "The Scottish government considers the proposed closure of the linear BBC Scotland channel to be wholly unacceptable, and we oppose such a move in the strongest possible terms."
In the letter, to the watchdog's chief executive Melanie Dawes and director for Scotland Glenn Preston, McAllan said she understood that broadcasters must adapt to evolve with audience habits.
But she added public service broadcasters had a "unique responsibility to ensure their services remain accessible and relevant".
McAllan continued: "Closure of the linear channel would also be impossible to reconcile with a supposed ambition to move power and decision-making away from London and towards audiences across the UK who are paying for the service.
"Many viewers continue to rely on linear television services, and any move away from those services risks disproportionately affecting audiences who are less likely to access content through online platforms."
The culture secretary added that plans to close the nightly News at Seven programme would be a "totally unacceptable reduction in nationally relevant journalism".
The closure of the programme is expected to see about 10 posts cut in addition to the 60 BBC Scotland announced earlier this year.
McAllan also called out a "disparity in indigenous language broadcasting" and highlighted the "total absence" of Commonwealth Games coverage on BBC One Scotland.
The BBC said a wide range of its programming currently shown on the linear TV channel would be available online or on BBC One or BBC Two in Scotland.
Shows include Scotland's Home of the Year, Murder Case, Inside Barlinnie, the Scottish Cup Final and Hogmanay.
The current plans won't see any changes to BBC Scotland's main news programme Reporting Scotland, which is shown on BBC One or the broadcasters radio or online services.
After the announcement, Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine said more cuts could be on the way.
The BBC previously announced it would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 - almost one in 10 jobs - as part of measures to make £500m savings in the next two years.
In June, 550 job cuts were announced in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage of cuts.
In recent months, the BBC announced a series of closures of programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus.
Cuts to radio programmes have also been announced.

title: Sam Fender pre-sale moved after 'bot attack'
content:
Sam Fender has rescheduled the pre-sale for his tour's homecoming show after a "sophisticated bot attack" reportedly affected a ticketing website.
In a post on Instagram, the 32-year-old said he had been told the site Gigantic had been hit for his shows at St James' Park in Newcastle in summer 2027, prompting him to move the sale back 24 hours to 09:30 GMT on Thursday.
It came days after he removed a ticket category from sale due to his unhappiness with the costs for fans, which he said were out of his control.
Gigantic said its system had detected an "unusually high volume of suspicious activity" resulting in error messages on its site and it had halted the pre-sale to protect fans.
Fender announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour last week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester.
The musician from North Shields did not give details for any other venues being affected by the "bot attack", but a source told the BBC they did not have any issues buying tickets for the London show.
Fender wrote: "Being told that there's been a sophisticated bot attack to the Gigantic ticket site which is impacting the St James' Park pre-sale.
"We're going to have to move the Newcastle pre-sale to 09:30 tomorrow to ensure real fans get the tickets."
Gigantic said in a statement: "We know how frustrating this morning was for many of you, and we're sorry.
"Fans should be able to buy tickets fairly, and that is what we're working to make sure happens."

title: 'Condemned as unnatural': 10 images of 19th-Century Parisian women who lived and dressed as men
content:
In 1800, women in Paris were banned from wearing trousers. Throughout the 19th and early 20th Century, many flouted or found a way around the law, rebelling against the stifling restrictions in order to dress – or in some cases live – as men. Here are 10 images capturing their distinctive style and their bravery.
During the French Revolution (1789-1799) many of the women of Paris had donned trousers to join male protestors on the barricades. Their hopes for liberty and equality on a par with men were expressed in the Declaration of the Rights of Women. Yet its author Olympe DeGouge went on to be guillotined in 1793, condemned as an "unnatural" woman.
In 1800 the wearing of trousers for women was banned in Paris "to put an end to the period when women were demanding rights and wishing to participate in the political life of their society," says Marine Kisiel, curator of new exhibition, A Wardrobe of One's Own: Dissident Femininities in the 19th Century, at the Palais Galliera in Paris.
French women in the 19th Century were expected to be content in the role of wife and mother. They were to be admired by painters and poets and defined by their feminine attire. But a great many French women rebelled against these strictures, particularly at the end of the 19th and early 20th Centuries, when the first wave of feminism coincided with a burgeoning lesbian subculture in Paris.
The fight for the right to wear male clothing is an overlooked chapter in the history of women's rights, perhaps no more so than in France. Masculine clothing gave women a sense of agency as they broke down barriers to enter universities and professions that had previously been excluded to them, or as they sought to freely express their sexuality. The press mocked them, the authorities cracked down, and the medical establishment condemned them as "inverts", but women continued to push for sartorial freedom. Here, we explore this history in 10 images.
Masculine fashion for women in France first appeared in the late 18th Century in the form of the riding habit, a style imported from England. Both the jacket and the women who wore them were known as Amazons, after the female warriors of Greek legend, suggesting that these agile, sporty women were viewed with both fascination and fear. As the century progressed, tailored jackets and coats became an increasingly important part of women's wardrobes.
While feminised versions of male styles were socially acceptable, wearing male clothing was not. This famously did not stop George Sand, the groundbreaking author and journalist who shunned gender conventions, living and loving as she chose. For Sand, wearing male clothing wasn't intended as a provocation, it was simply more practical. She wore it "to gain access to spaces reserved for men, such as the theatre stalls, because men's clothing was more economical than women's attire, and because she wished to enjoy freedom of movement and action," Kisiel tells the BBC.
Given the patriarchal nature of French 19th-Century society, it may come as a surprise to learn that a number of women took up arms. "Numerous accounts and photographic series exist, and we know it was a significant phenomenon," says Kisiel. They were excluded from joining the army proper but they were able to join the irregular volunteer corps. During the Franco-Prussian War, Marie-Antoinette Lix did just that, taking part in the defence of the Vosges department, and distinguishing herself during the Battle of Nompatelize.
Jane – or Jeanne – Dieulafoy also fought, alongside her husband Marcel, during the war. She took up masculine attire once again when the couple embarked on a series of archaeological excursions in Persia (now Iran). Thereafter Dieulafoy chose to dress in dapper men's suits, for which she managed to obtain a permit, although on what grounds remains unclear. This seems to have done nothing to prevent her becoming a major society figure. The couple hosted an exclusive salon and regularly socialised with both the French prime minister and president.
With concerns around women in male clothing growing towards the end of the century, masculinised lesbians bore the brunt of much of this hostility. "Through both their gender presentation and their sexuality, they doubly eluded heteropatriarchal male control," the art historian Lola Charnay tells the BBC. They were frequently caricatured by the press who "created a scapegoat for a collective imagination that oscillated between fascination with those who broke free from social norms, and a need to tame that defiance in order to maintain a degree of social control," says Charnay.
Although the rules against women wearing trousers were vigorously enforced at the time, cycling was the one activity where it was permitted (it was later extended to horse riding). However, not even this activity had escaped the male establishment's desire to intervene in every aspect of women's lives. Doctors had initially voiced concern, before concluding that it was good for women's health and would produce the vigorous mothers that France needed. Women, in contrast, simply saw it as a route to freedom and the bicycle became a powerful symbol of female emancipation in the Belle Époque.
The artist Rosa Bonheur, pictured here on the right, is one of the few women known to have been granted a permit to wear trousers for other reasons. Initially given one for health reasons when she accompanied her partner on a trip to the Pyrenees, she was later granted another for the abattoir visits which enabled her to conduct research for her animal paintings. Eventually "it became a part of her public profile, and she started to play up to it a little bit," says her biographer, Catherine Hewitt.
Despite the attitudes of society at large, Paris was home to a thriving lesbian subculture in the late 19th Century, and Mathilde de Morny, better known as Missy, was one of its leading lights. The daughter of the Duke of Morny, Missy had entered into a marriage of convenience with the Marquis de Belbeuf, who was himself homosexual, although the pair divorced in 1903. Openly lesbian, Missy adapted flamboyant masculine style and had an affair with the writer Colette who included a fictional version of her in the novel The Pure and the Impure.
The daughter of wealthy parents from the US, the artist Romaine Brooks spent much of her life in Paris where her long-term partner Nathalie Clifford Barney also lived. Sporting a short hairstyle and elegantly tailored masculine clothing, Brooks frequented a circle of equally wealthy, unconventional Europeans and Americans, many of whom were also creatively minded and lesbian. This 1920s self-portrait epitomises her refined, androgynous style.
However, the vast majority of lesbians who adopted male clothing were neither rich nor famous. They were simply ordinary women who wanted to assert their identity. Where and how they were able to dress as they chose "depended on their strategies, their 'passing,' and their social context. For a great many ordinary individuals, nothing is known due to a lack of archival records, yet photographs reveal that they constituted a multitude," says Kisiel.
The ban remained on the statute books for more than 200 years, and was formally repealed in 2013 – though it had been largely ignored for decades. Every Parisian woman who today thinks nothing of pulling on a pair of trousers owes these uncompromising women a debt of gratitude.
A Wardrobe of One's Own: Dissident Femininities in the 19th Century is at the Palais Galliera in Paris until 14 February 2027.

title: Russell Brand tells trial sexual consent is 'fundamental'
content:
Russell Brand has told the jury at his trial he believes sexual consent is "fundamental" and "more important than sex itself".
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.
Giving evidence on Wednesday, Brand said the allegations had been "deeply traumatic" and had a "devastating" impact on him.
The media personality gave evidence as his defence case began at his trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.
Asked whether consent was important to him, he told the court: "Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself."
Brand told the court he had previously been "comfortable" allowing his fame to "facilitate sexual access, which I agree with you was wrong".
But asked by the prosecution whether he "needed and was prepared to go to any lengths", Brand replied: "Absolutely no."
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC suggested to Brand there were inconsistencies between his previous prepared police statement and what he told the jury.
"Ms Karmy-Jones, I completely agree," he replied. "Since these events occurred there's been escalating recollection.
"It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life. I've focused on it at the expense of my marriage, my children and health.
"I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are inconsistent and I acknowledge that."
He said: "I do recognise I have been a very determined and focused man.
"With women, of course, which is the subject of my trial, I've been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering, and idiocy."
He told the jury: "Regrettably I've had a lot of consensual sex, which I see has caused harm."
After Brand entered the witness box on Wednesday morning, defence barrister Ian Winter KC began by taking him through the indictment, asking him if he had committed the offences.
After each question, Brand replied "no" loudly towards the jury.
Brand was then asked about the Channel 4 documentary and the impact it had on his relationships with friends and colleagues. "It was devastating," Brand said.
Winter questioned whether Brand had been able to persuade any friend or acquaintance who might have been able to give evidence on his behalf to appear in court.
Brand replied: "I have not." Winter asked: "Will they touch you with a bargepole?" Brand said: "No."

title: Celebrity Traitors' Joe Lycett's tribute to viral TikTok nan
content:
Celebrity Traitors star and comedian Joe Lycett has paid colourful tribute to the Welsh grandmother who went viral on TikTok after getting caught in shop shutters and being hoisted into the air.
The moment Anne Hughes was left dangling 7ft (2.1 metres) in the air was captured on CCTV - and viewed tens of millions of times on social media.
Lycett, who is also an artist and a fan of the viral video, painted the incident for his art exhibition at the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery.
Anne died in 2025 , but her granddaughter, Lilly Hughes, said Lycett's "lovely" painting has meant her nan's legacy has lived on and she would "have it on my wall any day".
The Everything Must Go exhibition is Lycett's first major solo art exhibition and is "about things which are no longer with us".
Lycett, who was banished from Celebrity Traitors for being too keen to be a traitor, said on Instagram: "My painting in tribute to the great Anne Hughes, who brought joy to millions when she was hoisted into the air outside the best-one she worked at in Rhondda Cynon Taf, Wales.
"She took the experience in good spirit, saying in an interview with the BBC, 'my grandchildren ask me why I am holding on to my trolley and I say I just don't know'."
Anne's interviews with BBC Wales and footage from the famous CCTV ended up being viewed at least 58 million times on the BBC News Instagram account alone.
Lilly, 28, who was very close to her grandmother, said: "I thought she's back from the dead, she's risen again and now my nan is in a museum.
"It's lovely, I would have it on my wall any day."
In the past 12 months, Lycett, 38, from Birmingham, has been producing works the museum has described as celebrating "nostalgia, grief and loss", from a sculpture of an extinct large woolly mammoth to an abstract painting of TV personality Cilla Black, who died in 2015.
The artwork, including Anne's moment, are painted in a child-like style and in bold and bright colours.
Lilly said her grandmother's legacy has lived on. She said: "Every time that it's mentioned people laugh about it. And then it just brings a smile to my face because I think 'oh nan, if you were here today'.
"It's absolutely hilarious, so it definitely helps with the grieving process."
The viral moment was previously immortalised by graffiti artist Tee2Sugars on the shutter she was caught on.
Lilly, who is a midwife and lives in Caerphilly, added: "Honestly if she was alive today she would say that the world has gone mad. I find Joe really funny and the fact that he's now painted my nan is a bit mind-blowing."
She also revealed her grandmother had told a "little fib" in her BBC interview about holding onto her trolley, and said she was in fact holding onto it because "she didn't want anyone stealing her fags".
Lilly says she still uses the story as an "ice breaker" in her work.
"I'll be looking after a woman and I will tell her about my nan and all of sudden I'm in the room with her whole family watching the video and they'll be absolutely peeing themselves. It's brilliant," she said.

title: Mum quits job as lawyer to voice Netflix cartoon
content:
A mum says she left her late-night legal career behind for voiceover work from home where she can care for her children.
Emily McGonagle started her working life as a lawyer in the capital, often finishing at 03:00, but started to question whether she could sustain it long term.
After having children, she decided to seek something "more flexible" than her daily commute from Colchester to Canary Wharf, and pivoted to voiceover work in 2019.
The 42-year-old voices eight characters for the children's television series Spike, which premiered on Netflix on 12 October and is its number one children's show on the site in the UK.
The cartoon began as a preschool animation on YouTube called Fire Spike!, which was about the adventures of a dragon and his friends.
It was created by a Lithuanian company called Bored Panda, founded in 2009.
When McGonagle joined the team, it had "less than 1,000 subscribers and minimal views".
It now has 1.25m subscribers and was the seventh most-watched Netflix show globally in its first week.
"It's insane," she said.
McGonagle's curiosity was stirred while her toddlers were watching television.
She said: "I just kind of always wondered about it, and then I was also watching a lot of kids' TV, like Paw Patrol and Peppa Pig, on repeat.
"I'd be like, 'Oh, that'll be such a cool job. I'd love to do that,' but how on earth do you get into it?'.
"I kind of just wrote it off because I don't have an acting background."
She told BBC Essex how she filled her home studio with professional audio equipment, and after several months of auditioning, got her first gig with Google.
She did commercials, signed up to some acting groups in Colchester and did a six-week acting course in London.
Three years ago she saw the advert for Spike.
"If you'd have asked me, when I was watching Peppa Pig all those years ago with my kids, that I'd be hearing my own voice on radio and Netflix, it would be beyond my wildest expectations."
Ahead of its Netflix debut, Bored Panda group's head of animation, Jonas Dovydaitis, said on social media he could not "get over how cool" that children around the world could now watch the show on the platform.

title: 6 Music Festival 2027 heads to Newcastle
content:
BBC Radio 6 Music has announced the 2027 edition of its annual festival will take place in Newcastle.
After four years in Greater Manchester, the festival will take place across Newcastle's independent and grassroots venues in March with five days of performances and DJ sets.
Tyneside last hosted the festival in 2015 but principal advisor for events and culture at Newcastle City Council, Jim Mawdsley, said since then "Newcastle has become a true music city".
Head of BBC Radio 6 Music Samantha Moy said: "The city and the region have such a rich musical legacy and a thriving creative community, which will make for another wonderful setting."
Newcastle has enjoyed recent success with national music events, having just hosted the Mercury Prize for the second year in a row.
The city also hosted the MOBO Awards in 2025.
The 6 Music Festival has been running since 2014 and initially was a roving event, moving around the country each year before settling in Manchester in 2023.
6 Music presenter Lauren Laverne said: "Having grown up in the North East, I know just how much music means to people here and the important role it plays in local culture and communities.

In 2026, the festival saw performances from the likes of Bloc Party, Courtney Barnett and Jacob Alon.
Mawdsley said: "Since it was last here, Newcastle has become a true music city with many of our artists being recognised not least by awards like the Mercury Prize, which has shortlisted Sam Fender, Jade and Knats in the last two years, but there is a real collaborative spirit in the city.
"We believe that our moment is now.
"Music is a vital element of our cultural lifeblood, and we can't wait to welcome 6 Music listeners to learn more about how vibrant the city has become."
6 Music Festival 2027 will take place 15-19 March and the full lineup and venues will be announced next year.

title: Neil Young sues Trump campaign again for playing Rockin' in the Free World at rally
content:
Rock veteran Neil Young has filed a $10m lawsuit against a fundraising committee that supports US President Donald Trump, citing "unauthorised" use of his 1989 song Rockin' in the Free World.
The Canadian-American star alleges that the Trump 47 Committee infringed on his copyright when it played the song before Trump took the stage at a 12 October rally in Ohio. Playing the song amounts to an "unauthorised public performance", the lawsuit says.
The singer-songwriter sued the Trump re-election campaign in 2020 over its use of the same song and Devil's Sidewalk. Young said the parties settled the matter shortly thereafter.
The White House referred to the Republican National Committee, who the BBC has contacted for comment.
Through his company Silver Fiddle Music, Young alleges that the song was played without a licence or Young's permission at a political event in Youngstown, Ohio on 12 October.
In the US, music used at campaign rallies often requires a public performance licence for it to be played for an audience, even if a campaign has already purchased a legal copy of the recording.
According to US Congress, because sound recordings do not have a general public-performance right, permission is only needed from the musical-work copyright holders, which can be obtained directly from the copyright holders themselves or through performing rights organisations.
The five-page federal lawsuit says that Trump "was personally aware that a licence would be required to play the Song at rallies," and that Young "has not, and would not, grant the required licence". It also says the song has been played "numerous times at other rallies".
The Grammy Award winner, 80, who has strongly opposed Trump's politics, characterises the song as "a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten".
Young says that the song is "the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for".
In 2020, Young sued Trump's re-election campaign for copyright infringement over the same song, as well as Devil's Sidewalk.
The new lawsuit claims that the campaign, at the time, "asserted no defence and immediately settled shortly after it was served", promising to never use the song without permission again.
Young posted about the lawsuit on his website on Tuesday, thanking Trump for coming to so many of his shows in the 1980s and 1990s, but stopped short of allowing him to play his music.
"I am sorry it came to this, but money and transactions are something you understand," he wrote.
Young, The Rolling Stones, Rihanna, Adele, REM and the estate of Prince have previously criticised the president for using their music at campaign events.

title: Family row over George Michael items up for auction - including Faith guitar
content:
A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.
The guitar played by the singer-songwriter in the Faith music video is one of several items being auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant.
Siobhan died in 2014 and the items are being sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.
Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Both Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.
Sworders describes the 32 lots as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".
Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.
Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.
Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.
There is no suggestion that Belcher does not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.
Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.
In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considers the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name is "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".
He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" is "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".
Bailey has asked that the auction should not go ahead, or, if it does, that it be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.
Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.
She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.
"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.
"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."
The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.
The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.
In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

title: Babydoll singer says life will 'never be the same again' after UK number one
content:
Jamie Miller says "nothing feels normal" anymore but he is trying to "live in the moment" as he comes to terms with his history-making song Babydoll.
Last week the 29-year-old became the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with the viral TikTok hit .
The singer, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, said his dreams had "come true" and life would "never be the same again" after a challenging few years in which he even had to give up on music for a time.
Miller said the last year had been "insane" as he has gone from watching Gavin and Stacey with his parents to getting messages on his social media from the cast.
Miller made history when he became the first Welsh artist to top the singles chart since Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.
He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone.
"It just doesn't feel real. To actually live my dreams the way that it's coming about right now," he said.
The song found fame on TikTok when actress Jennifer Love Hewitt posted videos featuring the track. But Miller said the "genuineness" of the track also made it stand out as his first song since his hiatus.
"I went through a really, really hard few years  in my personal life, and I took two years off music," he said.
"There's a genuineness to how I sound in the song. The world's in a little bit of a dark place right now so maybe that's why it's made people come together."
Miller's song has shot him to stardom but, of course, life carries on as normal for his loved ones.
He said his parents were "finding it a bit mad" with his dad going back to work as an Uber driver in Cardiff.
"None of us know what's going on," he said.
"I remember sitting on the couch with my mum and dad last Christmas and we were all watching Gavin and Stacey.
"Now Ruth Jones and James Corden are commenting on my posts."
Last weekend Miller and Off Campus star Antonio Cipriano brought Babydoll to Strictly Come Dancing which left the Welsh star feeling a "little emotional" as he reconnected with Emma Willis.
He describes the presenter as one of his "biggest champions" in the last decade. She previously hosted The Voice UK when Miller got to the final in 2017.
He added: "It felt fulfilling to go up to her and say that I made something of myself.
"I've watched Strictly Come Dancing growing up and that's obviously been such a dream of mine to perform on the show."
Miller said now he wanted to "marry the two worlds of dancing and singing" in his career.

title: Festival saved after new location approved
content:
Organisers of a festival threatened with closure say they "couldn't be more excited" after a licence was granted for it to move to a new site.
The Godney Gathering, which has featured artists such as UB40, The Darkness and Scouting for Girls, has been held at Garslade Farm, just outside Glastonbury, Somerset, since 2014.
The two-day festival is now set to move to nearby Woodford Farm after a licence was approved by Somerset Council.
Organiser Mike Daniells called the move "a new chapter" following an "emotional and challenging" journey since the Covid-19 pandemic.
According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS), the new licence allows one event to be held each year on the third Friday and Saturday in July.
It also allows the event to have a total capacity, which includes staff, contractors, performers and volunteers, of just under 10,000 people.
Daniells said the camping element of the festival, which originally began in 2011, had previously been provided independently by a local farmer, which Daniells said had made the event "financially unviable".
"We were at a crossroads of whether we had to cancel the event, suspend it forever or try to find a new location," he added.
Daniells said the new location meant both camping and entertainment would be under one roof.
Somerset councillor Marcus Kravis, who chaired the council meeting, said he was impressed by the event management plan for the festival, describing it as "comprehensive".
Several local residents objected the decision on the grounds of noise, traffic congestion and public nuisance.
Daniells said the festival has "always worked very positively with the local community".
Following the councils decision, Daniells thanked the festival's supporters for "being patient" and believing in them.
"It's hard to put into words what this moment means to us. The journey here has been emotional and challenging at times," he said.
"A new field, a new chapter ... bring on 2027," he added.

title: Sam Fender pre-sale moved after 'bot attack'
content:
Sam Fender has rescheduled the pre-sale for his tour's homecoming show after a "sophisticated bot attack" reportedly affected a ticketing website.
In a post on Instagram, the 32-year-old said he had been told the site Gigantic had been hit for his shows at St James' Park in Newcastle in summer 2027, prompting him to move the sale back 24 hours to 09:30 GMT on Thursday.
It came days after he removed a ticket category from sale due to his unhappiness with the costs for fans, which he said were out of his control.
Gigantic said its system had detected an "unusually high volume of suspicious activity" resulting in error messages on its site and it had halted the pre-sale to protect fans.
Fender announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour last week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester.
The musician from North Shields did not give details for any other venues being affected by the "bot attack", but a source told the BBC they did not have any issues buying tickets for the London show.
Fender wrote: "Being told that there's been a sophisticated bot attack to the Gigantic ticket site which is impacting the St James' Park pre-sale.
"We're going to have to move the Newcastle pre-sale to 09:30 tomorrow to ensure real fans get the tickets."
Gigantic said in a statement: "We know how frustrating this morning was for many of you, and we're sorry.
"Fans should be able to buy tickets fairly, and that is what we're working to make sure happens."

title: Why Rugby is honouring hometown hero 'Mr Music'
content:
A plaque dedicated to Rugby musician Tom Ward, known in his hometown as "Mr Music", is to be unveiled in a Warwickshire park.
Born in 1913, the musician founded his first band, The Harmo Boys, as a 16-year-old at Lawrence Sheriff School.
He went on to spend four decades playing big-band-style dance music for audiences in Rugby, across Warwickshire and the West Midlands, and, on one occasion, for a nationwide audience.
His son Keith Ward, who has led efforts to get a permanent memorial to his father, said: "He was also a co-founder of the Rugby Theatre and started the town's RAG (Raise and Give) Festival, which is still going. He'd be very proud of the memorial."
A plaque honouring Tom will be unveiled near the bandstand at Whitehall Rec in Rugby on 28 October.
The current Lawrence Sheriff School band will perform in tribute to Tom, who founded the school's first band and contributed greatly to the town.
Tom was a saxophonist and formed his first band while at school, despite coming from a family with no musical background.
After leaving Lawrence Sheriff School, he joined British Thompson-Houston (BTH), an electrical engineering firm in Rugby, rather than pursuing music full-time.
"He started there in 1935 as an apprentice and founded the RAG [Raise and Give] Festival that still exists in the town," said Keith.
"The first £500 they raised went to the local hospital, and I was told that the first collection was in coppers."
"They were carrying it down to the bank, and the bottom fell out of the box."
However, his love of music endured. He opened a music shop on Regents Street and led the Tom Ward Band, earning a reputation as Rugby's "Mr Music".
Tom played a variety of instruments, could read music but was best known for his saxophone work.
His music took him across the country, performing big-band dance music at venues in Jersey and Great Yarmouth, at the Dorchester in London, and closer to home at Coventry's Leofric Hotel and the Laurels in Rugby.
He even had a brush with fame.
After winning a regional National Dance Band competition in the 1930s, he was invited in 1947 to perform on the BBC radio programme Industry Entertains, hosted by comedian Kenneth Horne.
Tom travelled from Rugby to the GEC Club in Coventry to perform a three-minute solo for £6 - about £187 in 2026.
"In those days that was a lot of money," said Keith.
"I think the main thing is it took a lot of working to convince them that, you know, could he possibly go to this?
"There were a lot of words in the right direction in those days to say, 'Yes, I'm representing Rugby; I need to go,' because there was also a rehearsal as well."

title: The blind musician singing in the face of adversity
content:
An award-winning singer, who was born with severely impaired vision, has said there is "so much that can be gained by inclusion and diversity".
Folk musician Elena Piras is originally from Sardinia, Italy, and now lives in Charlbury, Oxfordshire, where she has recorded her latest single.
In addition to her visual disability, she was also left with severe hearing loss after being caught up in the 7/7 London bombings in 2005.
Speaking to the BBC, she said she continues to pursue her music career despite the obstacles and is now fundraising for her third album.
Piras sang in choirs from the age of seven and has performed on national TV in Italy.
She said she came to England in 1995 at the age of 18, after finding out about The Royal National College for the Blind in Hereford.
"I knew that the opportunities for visually impaired people in my country were not amazing," she said. "We had very, very basic provision for anything and it was a fight to obtain it as well."
While her parents were "not very happy" about the move, Piras said she always wanted to be "as independent as possible".
Piras said her visual impairment was "part of my life, but it's not my life", adding that people were "not even willing to listen to what I can do".
She said: "I really didn't know that there was a problem with me being blind and music, maybe my talent always gave me the bypass.
"People saw my visual impairment first and they still do. As soon as they discovered that, they closed their eyes.
"We have legislation in this country that should help, but it's not implemented and that is a real shame for everybody because there's so much that can be gained by inclusion and diversity in every single field."
On 7 July 2005, Piras was at King's Cross Station and heard the blast of the Piccadilly Line bomb as it detonated in the tunnel between the station and Russell Square.
She said: "It was just a nightmare day and I remember someone trying to put me in a taxi.
"The first taxi driver didn't want to travel to the area where I lived because it was too close."
Afterwards, she said she started to become "very irritated" in noisy places and had difficulty harmonising when she sang.
She moved to Scotland and a hearing test in Glasgow showed she had lost 60% of her hearing, she said, adding: "For someone who's visually impaired, that's a lot."
The musician went on to live in the Highlands, and later in the Shetlands, where she studied Scots and Gaelic traditional music.
She said: "I really wanted to learn it and I discovered that singing in a language, especially in Gaelic, it wasn't enough - I had to learn the language if I wanted to sing at a certain level.
"It was just incredible. I met so many amazing people and learned so much."

title: Sheffield music 'really healthy', says Cabaret Voltaire veteran
content:
The future of Sheffield music looks "really healthy", one of Cabaret Voltaire's founding members has said after winding up the band's 50-year career in the city.
Chris Watson joined fellow founder Stephen Mallinder at the city's Octagon Centre on Sunday night to complete their UK-wide tour and finish where they had started in the mid-1970s.
The sold-out homecoming marks the end of a band that was at the forefront of a revolution in popular music, which saw musicians turn away from guitars towards wire-sprouting modular synthesisers and bedroom laptops.
Speaking to the BBC after the show, Watson said there was "a really good atmosphere" at the Octagon with "a lot of love in the room".
About finishing in Sheffield, he said: "It was perfect. I mean, we started there 50 years ago so that's the place we were always going to finish it and that's our, for Mal and I, the two remaining members, that's our home city so we were certain that's where we wanted to close the chapter."
The third founding member, Richard H Kirk, died in 2021.
Sheffield music journalist Daniel Dylan Wray, who was at the final show, said the band's influence had been "incalculable".
"They were originators and pioneers, doing it years ahead of everyone else, and blazing a trail that many others would follow," he said.
"The world of electronic, dance, industrial and post-punk music as we know it today was shaped by their output – everything from Detroit techno to groups like Nine Inch Nails via Sheffield's own rich lineage of electronic music, has all been touched and moulded by their greatness."
Cabaret Voltaire took their name from the Zurich club that became the birthplace of the Dadaist art movement in 1916.
German artist Hugo Ball, who travelled to Switzerland amid the horrors of World War One, teamed up with other emigres to perform anarchic, prank-like shows.
Its influence spread across Western artistic styles throughout the 20th Century and its rambunctious energy was adopted by artists looking to cause chaos and flip entrenched assumptions of what art should be.
For the Sheffield trio, whose early experiments sound akin to a sentient synthesiser having a nightmare, the Dadaists were an open door towards a performance style which some audiences found difficult to accept.
At one of their first shows, which Watson said the band had "blagged" at the University of Sheffield's students' union, they "confronted" an audience who were expecting disco.
He said the students were "ironically, people who you would think are front-thinking, people who would be interested in something new, and of course they weren't".
The musician added: "They were outraged by something that they couldn't think they could dance to, and so it just descended into this beautiful chaos, which we were really proud of."
Sonically, Watson drew on Sheffield's soundscapes, and he was also inspired by musique concréte, an art form that developed in France in the 1940s as a way of turning raw environmental sounds into musical compositions.
This led him to a career in producing sound for BBC radio and wildlife documentaries with Sir David Attenborough after he left the band in 1981.
He described the final Cabaret Voltaire tour as a celebration, rather than a reunion, because of Kirk's absence.
Nick Potter, a music programme producer at the University of Sheffield, said: "'It was a real honour to be able to host Cabaret Voltaire for their final ever gig - metres away from where they played their first in the students' union's Upper Refectory.

title: Nineties theme bar Wannabe planned in city centre
content:
A 90s-themed nostalgia bar named Wannabe after the debut hit of the Spice Girls is set to open in Lincoln city centre if plans are approved.
Developers said the new bar at the former Cognito restaurant in Park Street would be built entirely around "the best decade ever".
The bar - named after the 1996 single which propelled the Spice Girls to worldwide fame - plans to open in December.
Promoted as "Lincoln's new 90s throwback bar", with neon lights and big tunes, it is also advertising for staff.
A licensing application seeks to approve changes to the floor layout and bar length.
Anyone wishing to comment on the application should contact the licensing team at City of Lincoln Council by 4 November.
Cognito closed the premises in January and relocated to the Pyewipe pub, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

Young says that the song is "the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for".
In 2020, Young sued Trump's re-election campaign for copyright infringement over the same song, as well as Devil's Sidewalk.
The new lawsuit claims that the campaign, at the time, "asserted no defence and immediately settled shortly after it was served", promising to never use the song without permission again.
Young posted about the lawsuit on his website on Tuesday, thanking Trump for coming to so many of his shows in the 1980s and 1990s, but stopped short of allowing him to play his music.
"I am sorry it came to this, but money and transactions are something you understand," he wrote.
Young, The Rolling Stones, Rihanna, Adele, REM and the estate of Prince have previously criticised the president for using their music at campaign events.

title: Government minister calls for review of 'unacceptable' BBC Scotland channel closure
content:
Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan has urged Ofcom to review "wholly unacceptable" plans to close the linear BBC Scotland channel.
The BBC last week announced the dedicated Scotland channel - as well as BBC Three and Radio 4 Extra - would move online as part of measures to make £500m of savings by 2028.
McAllan said moving the channel online would "reverse progress in improving the visibility and representation of Scotland within the UK's broadcasting landscape".
She called on Ofcom, the UK's independent broadcasting regulator, to scrutinise the decision and its implications.
McAllan wrote: "The Scottish government considers the proposed closure of the linear BBC Scotland channel to be wholly unacceptable, and we oppose such a move in the strongest possible terms."
In the letter, to the watchdog's chief executive Melanie Dawes and director for Scotland Glenn Preston, McAllan said she understood that broadcasters must adapt to evolve with audience habits.
But she added public service broadcasters had a "unique responsibility to ensure their services remain accessible and relevant".
McAllan continued: "Closure of the linear channel would also be impossible to reconcile with a supposed ambition to move power and decision-making away from London and towards audiences across the UK who are paying for the service.
"Many viewers continue to rely on linear television services, and any move away from those services risks disproportionately affecting audiences who are less likely to access content through online platforms."
The culture secretary added that plans to close the nightly News at Seven programme would be a "totally unacceptable reduction in nationally relevant journalism".
The closure of the programme is expected to see about 10 posts cut in addition to the 60 BBC Scotland announced earlier this year.
McAllan also called out a "disparity in indigenous language broadcasting" and highlighted the "total absence" of Commonwealth Games coverage on BBC One Scotland.
The BBC said a wide range of its programming currently shown on the linear TV channel would be available online or on BBC One or BBC Two in Scotland.
Shows include Scotland's Home of the Year, Murder Case, Inside Barlinnie, the Scottish Cup Final and Hogmanay.
The current plans won't see any changes to BBC Scotland's main news programme Reporting Scotland, which is shown on BBC One or the broadcasters radio or online services.
After the announcement, Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine said more cuts could be on the way.
The BBC previously announced it would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 - almost one in 10 jobs - as part of measures to make £500m savings in the next two years.
In June, 550 job cuts were announced in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage of cuts.
In recent months, the BBC announced a series of closures of programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus.
Cuts to radio programmes have also been announced.

title: Mum quits job as lawyer to voice Netflix cartoon
content:
A mum says she left her late-night legal career behind for voiceover work from home where she can care for her children.
Emily McGonagle started her working life as a lawyer in the capital, often finishing at 03:00, but started to question whether she could sustain it long term.
After having children, she decided to seek something "more flexible" than her daily commute from Colchester to Canary Wharf, and pivoted to voiceover work in 2019.
The 42-year-old voices eight characters for the children's television series Spike, which premiered on Netflix on 12 October and is its number one children's show on the site in the UK.
The cartoon began as a preschool animation on YouTube called Fire Spike!, which was about the adventures of a dragon and his friends.
It was created by a Lithuanian company called Bored Panda, founded in 2009.
When McGonagle joined the team, it had "less than 1,000 subscribers and minimal views".
It now has 1.25m subscribers and was the seventh most-watched Netflix show globally in its first week.
"It's insane," she said.
McGonagle's curiosity was stirred while her toddlers were watching television.
She said: "I just kind of always wondered about it, and then I was also watching a lot of kids' TV, like Paw Patrol and Peppa Pig, on repeat.
"I'd be like, 'Oh, that'll be such a cool job. I'd love to do that,' but how on earth do you get into it?'.
"I kind of just wrote it off because I don't have an acting background."
She told BBC Essex how she filled her home studio with professional audio equipment, and after several months of auditioning, got her first gig with Google.
She did commercials, signed up to some acting groups in Colchester and did a six-week acting course in London.
Three years ago she saw the advert for Spike.
"If you'd have asked me, when I was watching Peppa Pig all those years ago with my kids, that I'd be hearing my own voice on radio and Netflix, it would be beyond my wildest expectations."
Ahead of its Netflix debut, Bored Panda group's head of animation, Jonas Dovydaitis, said on social media he could not "get over how cool" that children around the world could now watch the show on the platform.

title: Documentary tells story of city's Muslim community
content:
A Gloucester filmmaker has made a documentary that details the history and experiences of the city's Muslim population.
Mohamed Husain Jaffer, who has lived in Gloucester since 1977, spent months planning, filming and editing a new documentary called Eid in Gloucester with the intention of not only capturing the atmosphere of Eid, but also the stories, history and experiences of Muslims who have made Gloucester their home.
Jaffer said he wanted to capture how the community had grown since he arrived in the city.
He says that "although Gloucester is small, it has a big heart as many communities fit in it".
Jaffer's film documents the memories from first generation Muslims to the present day. One contributor, Zuleikha Kadodia, reflects on how Eid was celebrated in Gloucester decades ago.
"In the early days there were no mosques in Gloucester," she said, having lived there since 1969.
"The first generation performed their daily prayers in small, rented properties. Imams led prayers in these spaces and Eid was celebrated quietly at home with family members reflecting the size of the community."
Director of Gloucester Feed the Hungry, Hashim Norat, described realising the importance within the community of his father - who he said was responsible for introducing the first Islamic prayer room to the city.
Norat's father was a first generation Muslim who arrived in Gloucester in the early to mid 1960s.
"As a child," Norat said, "Eid was always very special. Waking up in the morning and having agarbatti [incense stick] lit and Mashallah and kusbara going around the house, we knew it was Eid.
"Another beauty of Eid was everybody, the family, the extended family, everybody was together. The children and the grandchildren, the magic was everyone being there together."
Norat's father converted the cellar of their house into a Salah room, or Islamic prayer room - which he said was the first in the city.
On his father's death bed, there was a line of Alims [Islamic scholars] that his father had taught over the years. They were all praying quietly into his ear, one after another.
"It was at that point that I truly realised who my father was. He was the baji [father] of the community. Not many people like him have come along."
Since the days of gatherings for prayer in people's homes, the Muslim population in Gloucester grew and it was clear there was a need for a permanent site.
Through much fundraising in the community, the first purpose-built mosque was completed in 1983 in Ryecroft Street.
In the 1960s, one of the city's first Eid congregations was held in Gloucester Park and Eid celebrations still take pace there today. Jaffer's film shows drone footage of Eid celebrations earlier this year.
"While Eid is celebrated in the many mosques across Gloucester, it also comes alive in Gloucester Park," he said.
"People come together as one community, people come from all over the region to be part of the special day."
Jaffer's film, Eid in Gloucester, will be shown at Gloucester Guildhall on 19 January 2027.
